title: Lyrical Ballads
author: William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge
setting: The Quantock Hills and the Wye valley in the summer of 1798; the Cumberland and Westmorland vales of the 1800 volume; and, in the Mariner, a voyage to the southern ice and back
lengthNote: Thirty-six poems in the Astor selection, from ballads of a few stanzas to the long blank-verse narratives of Tintern Abbey and Michael
openingLine: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three:
summary: A small anonymous volume printed in Bristol in 1798 put a ghost-ship ballad in deliberately old-fashioned spelling next to conversations with a beggar, a child who will not agree that her dead siblings are gone, and an old huntsman who cannot cut a root. Its short Advertisement called the poems experiments in the language of ordinary people. The 1800 enlargement doubled the book, added the Preface that turned the experiment into a theory, moved the Mariner from the front of the volume to the back, and filled a second volume with Lucy, Michael and the Cumberland beggar. The Astor edition prints each poem as it first entered the book, so the collection can be read as what it was: two poets testing, in public, what a poem is allowed to sound like.
referenceStyle: poem title, with the part or stanza number where the corpus divides a poem; the text prints no line numbers

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Lyrical Ballads (the two-volume text of 1800)
sourceText.note: Quotations follow the 1800 wording, in which Coleridge’s poem is headed ‘The Ancient Mariner’ and the archaic spelling of the 1798 ‘Ancyent Marinere’ has been modernised. The Astor edition prints the 1798 form of that poem, so readers will find small differences of spelling and some altered lines. The poem beginning ‘A slumber did my spirit seal’ is printed in this text without a heading of its own, directly after ‘She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways’.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Anonymously, in Bristol, by Joseph Cottle. A short Advertisement calls most of the poems experiments.

atAGlance.label: Enlarged
atAGlance.note: Two volumes, the second entirely new, with the Preface that became the book’s manifesto.

atAGlance.label: Coleridge’s share
atAGlance.note: The Preface names the Ancient Mariner, the Foster-Mother’s Tale, the Nightingale and Love as the work of a Friend.

atAGlance.label: Astor selection
atAGlance.note: Drawn from both editions, each in the form in which it first appeared.

structure.label: The Ancient Mariner
structure.title: A wedding-guest detained by a story he did not ask for
structure.summary: An old sailor stops one of three guests on his way to a wedding and holds him with his eye. The tale he tells runs from a becalmed ship to the southern ice, a shot albatross, a ship of Death and Life-in-Death, a crew who die and rise, water-snakes blessed without meaning to, and a return home that leaves the teller condemned to tell it again. The guest misses the feast and goes home a sadder and a wiser man. In 1798 the poem opened the book; in 1800 Wordsworth moved it to the end of the first volume, just before Tintern Abbey.

structure.label: Encounters and conversations (1798)
structure.title: Adults who ask questions and are answered
structure.summary: The shorter 1798 poems are mostly meetings: a friend rebuked for sitting on a stone, a child who counts her dead brother and sister among the living, a boy who invents a reason because his father demands one, an old huntsman weeping over a severed root. Expostulation and Reply, The Tables Turned, We Are Seven, Anecdote for Fathers, Simon Lee and Lines Written in Early Spring share a plain stanza and a speaker who learns more than he teaches.

structure.label: The Thorn, The Idiot Boy and the tales of 1798
structure.title: Narrators who do not know what happened
structure.summary: The longer ballads of 1798 give their stories to speakers whose knowledge is partial. The Thorn is told by a garrulous man who has measured a pond and a moss-heap and can report only what the village says about Martha Ray. The Idiot Boy follows Betty Foy through a night of searching for a son who has been enjoying the owls. Goody Blake and Harry Gill, The Last of the Flock, The Female Vagrant and The Mad Mother put the poor and the abandoned at the centre of a page usually reserved for other people.

structure.label: Tintern Abbey
structure.title: Five years, a river and a sister
structure.summary: The poem that closed the 1798 volume is dated in its title to a July walking tour and is addressed, in its final movement, to the sister standing beside the speaker. It moves from the cliffs and hedge-rows in front of him to what those forms have done for him in lonely rooms in cities, then to a presence in setting suns and the mind of man, and finally to a prayer that Dorothy will carry the place in memory after he cannot. It is blank verse, not ballad, and it is where the collection’s theory of memory is worked out.

structure.label: The Lucy poems and the lyrics of 1800
structure.title: A girl who dies between stanzas
structure.summary: Written in the winter Wordsworth spent in Goslar and printed in the second volume, the Lucy poems are short, unexplained and final: a lover rides towards a cottage and fears a death that the poem never confirms; a violet by a mossy stone is in her grave; a slumber seals the speaker’s spirit and Lucy is rolled round with rocks and stones and trees. Nutting, There Was a Boy and Lucy Gray belong with them as poems in which a child or a wood is entered and something is lost.

structure.label: Michael and the rural narratives of 1800
structure.title: A sheep-fold left unfinished
structure.summary: The second volume ends with a pastoral in blank verse about a Grasmere shepherd who sends his son to the city to clear a debt on the land and asks him first to lay the corner-stone of a sheep-fold as a covenant. Luke goes to the bad, and Michael goes to the fold for seven years without lifting another stone. The Old Cumberland Beggar, The Brothers, Hart-Leap Well and the Poems on the Naming of Places share its concern with what a place remembers when the people are gone.

characters.name: The Ancient Mariner
characters.role: Teller of the tale, once a sailor on a ship that went south
characters.summary: A grey-bearded man with a glittering eye and a skinny hand who shot the bird his shipmates had welcomed and then watched them die for it. He is not explained: the killing has no motive in the poem, the blessing of the water-snakes is done unaware, and the penance is a compulsion to tell. He knows the face of the man who must hear him.
characters.clue: He stops one guest in three, holds him with his eye rather than his hand, and has been walking from land to land with a story that burns until it is told.

characters.name: The Wedding-Guest
characters.role: Next of kin to the bridegroom, stopped on the way to the feast
characters.summary: He begins by threatening the old man with his staff and ends by sitting on a stone like a three years’ child. He interrupts twice, beating his breast when he hears the bassoon and the bride pass, and is terrified once, when he decides the Mariner must be a ghost. He never reaches the wedding, and the last stanzas are about him, not the sailor.
characters.clue: He can hear the bassoon and see the bride go by, and still cannot choose but hear; he rises the next morning a different man.

characters.name: The Hermit of the wood
characters.role: A holy man who lives by the sea and rows out to the returning ship
characters.summary: He kneels at morn and noon and eve on a cushion of moss and loves to talk with sailors from far countries. He is the poem’s only church, and when the Mariner begs to be shriven his answer is a question: what manner of man are you? The Mariner’s answer is the whole tale, told for the first time.
characters.clue: His cushion is the moss on an oak-stump, his pilot faints and his pilot’s boy goes mad, and he crosses his brow before asking what kind of man has come ashore.

characters.name: The little cottage girl of We Are Seven
characters.role: An eight-year-old met near a churchyard
characters.summary: She has thick curls, a woodland air and a family of seven: two at Conway, two at sea, and two in the churchyard twelve steps from her mother’s door, where she knits, hems and eats her supper. The adult’s arithmetic makes no impression on her at all, and the poem lets her have the last word.
characters.clue: She sits and sings by two green graves, takes her porringer there after sunset, and will not subtract the dead from her count.

characters.name: Simon Lee
characters.role: An old huntsman of Cardigan, now the poorest man in his village
characters.summary: He ran with the hounds for twenty-five years in a blue livery-coat, outran men and horses, and is left with one eye, swollen ankles and a scrap of enclosed heath he cannot till. The poem promises a tale and refuses to supply one; what it gives instead is a single blow of a mattock and an old man’s tears.
characters.clue: One eye, a cherry cheek, a livery-coat fair behind and fair before, and a root of rotten wood he could have worked at for ever.

characters.name: Martha Ray
characters.role: The woman who sits by the thorn crying misery
characters.summary: Jilted on her wedding morning by Stephen Hill, pregnant, and then seen without a child, she goes to the mountain-top in every weather and is heard crying the same words. Whether she killed the baby, whether it lies under the moss, whether the pond shows its face, are all things the narrator has heard and cannot confirm. She is the poem’s subject and never its speaker.
characters.clue: A scarlet cloak, a thorn, a pond and a hill of moss; everybody in the village has a theory about her and nobody has asked her.

characters.name: Betty Foy
characters.summary: She sends her son on the pony to fetch the doctor for a sick neighbour and spends the night searching for him, swinging between terror and fury and back to joy. The poem gives her far more feeling than it gives the emergency, and her reunion with Johnny in the moonlight is treated as the real event of the night.
characters.clue: She fiddle-faddles with girt and stirrup at eight o’clock, sends her boy into the moonlight, and by midnight is running through the wood calling his name.

characters.name: Johnny Foy
characters.summary: Sent for a doctor, he lets the pony go where it likes and spends the night beside a waterfall under the owls. Asked what he saw, he reports that the cocks crowed to-whoo and the sun shone cold, and the narrator calls it his glory. The poem is one of the collection’s deliberate provocations: a subject other readers would have thought unfit for verse, given the last word.
characters.clue: He burrs like a mill, holds a branch of holly, and tells the truest account of a night out that anyone in the book gives.

characters.name: Lucy
characters.role: The girl of the Goslar lyrics
characters.summary: She lives by the springs of Dove where nobody praises her, is compared to a violet and a single star, and dies between one stanza and the next. Nothing about her is given but her effect on the speaker, which is the point: the poems record a difference rather than a person, and the last of them does not even name her.
characters.clue: A violet by a mossy stone, half-hidden; three years she grew; now she is rolled round with rocks and stones and trees.
characters.firstAppearance: Strange Fits of Passion I Have Known

characters.name: Michael
characters.role: A shepherd of Grasmere Vale, eighty-four years old
characters.summary: Stout of heart and strong of limb, frugal, and bound to his fields by a lifetime of work, he chooses to send his son away rather than sell half the land. The sheep-fold he asks Luke to begin is a covenant, and when the news of Luke’s ruin comes he goes on going to it for seven years without laying another stone. Wordsworth makes him a study of how love endures what it cannot mend.
characters.clue: He sends his only son to the city to save the land, asks him to lay one stone first, and is seen for years afterwards sitting by a heap he never finishes.

characters.name: Luke
characters.role: Michael’s son, sent to the city
characters.summary: A boy of eighteen who has been his father’s companion on the hills since he could walk, he lays the corner-stone as asked, writes loving letters for a while, and then gives himself to evil courses and disappears beyond the seas. The poem does not follow him: his fall is reported in three lines so that the weight can stay with the man who waits.
characters.clue: He lays the first stone of a sheep-fold with his own hands, goes down the public way with a bold face, and is never seen in the valley again.

characters.name: The Old Cumberland Beggar
characters.role: An aged man who makes a fixed round of the parish for alms
characters.summary: He sits on a step by the highway eating scraps from a flour-whitened bag while crumbs fall to the birds. Wordsworth has known him from childhood and he seems no older. The poem argues that his round creates the kindness it lives on, and asks that he be spared the workhouse and allowed to die under the sky.
characters.clue: The horseman stops to lodge a coin safely in his hat, the toll-gate keeper lifts the latch for him, and he has been exactly this old for as long as anyone remembers.

characters.name: The Sister of Tintern Abbey
characters.role: The dearest Friend addressed in the last movement of the poem
characters.summary: Unnamed in the poem, she is Dorothy Wordsworth, who walked the Wye with her brother in July 1798. He hears his former self in her voice and sees it in her wild eyes, and turns the end of the poem into a prayer that her memory will keep the place, and him, when he is gone. She is the reason the poem can promise that nature never did betray the heart that loved her.
characters.clue: She says nothing, but her wild eyes and her voice give the speaker back the self he says he has lost, and the poem ends by asking her to remember it.

themes.name: Nature as teacher and as indifference
themes.summary: The Tables Turned tells its friend to shut his books and take one impulse from a vernal wood, and Tintern Abbey builds a whole moral life on what setting suns and the living air have done for the speaker. But the Mariner’s ocean rots and shines without caring who watches, and the Lucy who is rolled round with rocks and stones has become part of a nature that no longer feels. The collection holds both views and does not choose.
themes.development: Argued in the two Esthwaite poems of 1798, made autobiography in Tintern Abbey, and turned over in 1800, where Nutting ends in a pang of guilt and the Lucy lyrics end in a grave.

themes.name: Memory and the five years
themes.summary: Tintern Abbey counts five years, five summers, five long winters, and then explains what a remembered landscape has been worth in lonely rooms and cities. The Preface says poetry takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity, and the collection keeps testing the claim: Michael is a story attached to a heap of stones so that the stones will remember, and the sister is asked to hold the Wye in mind for a brother who may not be there.
themes.development: Introduced as recompense in Tintern Abbey, theorised in the 1800 Preface, and made a duty in Michael, where the unfinished fold is the memory that outlives the family.

themes.name: The real language of men
themes.summary: The Preface promises incidents from common life told in a selection of the language really used by men, and the poems act on it: a huntsman’s swollen ankles, a girl’s porringer, a mattock and a stump of rotten wood. The Mariner runs the other way, in ballad archaisms Wordsworth never used, which is why the collaboration looks so odd from inside its own manifesto.
themes.development: Announced in the 1798 Advertisement, defended at length in the 1800 Preface, and contradicted by the book’s longest and best-known poem.

themes.name: Who is speaking, and what do they know
themes.summary: Half the poems are reports by people who saw part of something. The Thorn’s narrator has measured the pond and the moss-heap but relies on what the village says for everything that matters; the adult in We Are Seven has counted correctly and lost the argument; Simon Lee’s visitor admits there is no tale. The reader is repeatedly given the evidence and the witness together and asked to weigh the second.
themes.development: A comic problem in Anecdote for Fathers and We Are Seven, a moral one in The Thorn, and a permanent condition in the Mariner, who can only teach his tale, not prove it.

themes.name: Guilt, penance and the tale that must be told
themes.summary: The Mariner kills a bird for no stated reason and is punished with a compulsion to speak. The collection returns to the pattern in smaller keys: the boy in Nutting who ravages a hazel bower and feels the intruding sky, the speaker of Simon Lee left mourning by gratitude, Michael, who wonders whether he judged ill for his son. Guilt here is rarely for a crime; it is for a failure of feeling, discovered afterwards.
themes.development: Given supernatural machinery in the Mariner, then stripped of it in 1800, where the pain of Nutting has no albatross to hang round anyone’s neck.

themes.name: Poverty and responsibility
themes.summary: The beggar on his round, the shepherd who sells no land, the last of the flock, the female vagrant, the old man who cannot sever a root: the collection is a record of rural poverty in the 1790s and of what it asks of the person who happens to be watching. The Old Cumberland Beggar argues outright against the workhouse; Michael watches an inheritance go into a stranger’s hand. The poems are not remedies, and the discomfort of the observer is part of the subject.
themes.development: Present as encounter in 1798, when the speaker helps or fails to help, and as history in 1800, when whole households are followed to their end.

techniques.name: The ballad stanza
techniques.definition: A four-line stanza alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhymed on the second and fourth, inherited from the popular ballads collected in the eighteenth century.
techniques.inThisBook: The Mariner uses it for a ghost story and We Are Seven for an argument about arithmetic; the same tune carries the supernatural and the ordinary, which is the book’s central experiment.

techniques.name: Blank verse
techniques.definition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, the metre of Milton and of the English stage.
techniques.inThisBook: Tintern Abbey, Michael and The Old Cumberland Beggar use it for meditation and rural narrative rather than epic, and the long sentences that cross line-endings are where the collection thinks rather than sings.

techniques.name: The line that comes back
techniques.definition: A phrase repeated at intervals so that its meaning changes with its position.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘Water, water, every where’ is doubled inside one stanza; ‘we are seven’ closes the child’s every reply; the Mariner’s guest ‘cannot choose but hear’ twice before the tale has properly begun.

techniques.name: Speaking to the reader
techniques.definition: A poem that turns from its subject to the person reading it.
techniques.inThisBook: Simon Lee stops to tell its gentle Reader that no tale will be related and invites them to make one; Michael opens by telling you where to turn off the public way. The reader is made a participant rather than an audience.

techniques.name: The unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A speaker whose account the reader has reason to doubt or to weigh.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator of The Thorn measures the pond, reports the rumours, and admits he cannot tell how it may be; Wordsworth’s 1800 note explains that the poem is meant to show how superstition works in a loquacious mind.

techniques.name: Archaic diction
techniques.definition: Old spellings, verb forms and words used to make a poem sound as if it came from an earlier age.
techniques.inThisBook: The Mariner’s stoppeth, quoth, eftsoons and shrieve make it a pastiche of the old ballads; in 1798 the spelling was older still, and Wordsworth had it modernised in 1800, as this text shows.

techniques.name: Landscape as record
techniques.definition: A place described so that it carries the history of the people who lived in it.
techniques.inThisBook: Michael begins with a heap of unhewn stones you might pass by and ends with the same heap; Tintern Abbey reads five years off cliffs and hedge-rows; the Poems on the Naming of Places attach private history to rocks and pools.

quotations.text: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three:
quotations.context: The first two lines of the poem, and of the 1798 volume.
quotations.analysis: The verb is in an old third-person form and the article is indefinite: this is a mariner, any mariner, met by chance. One in three is the arithmetic of a folk-tale, and it tells the reader at once that the person stopped was not chosen for any reason he could know.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part I

quotations.text: He holds him with his glittering eye⁠— The wedding-guest stood still And listens like a three years’ child; The Mariner hath his will.
quotations.context: The guest has threatened the old man with his staff; the Mariner lets go of his arm.
quotations.analysis: The hand is released and the eye takes over, which is the moment the poem stops being about a nuisance and becomes about a spell. The guest sits like a child of three, an image of complete receptivity, and the tense shifts to the present so that the reader is held at the same moment he is.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part I

quotations.text: “God save thee, ancient Mariner! From the fiends that plague thee thus!⁠— Why look’st thou so?”⁠—“With my cross bow I shot the Albatross.”
quotations.context: The end of Part I: the guest sees something in the old man’s face and asks what fiends plague him.
quotations.analysis: The confession is four words at the end of a part, with no reason attached, and the poem never supplies one. The guest’s prayer and the Mariner’s answer share a single stanza, so the question and the crime arrive in one breath; the killing is disclosed as a thing already done, never as a decision.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part I

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, And all the boards did shrink; Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
quotations.context: The ship becalmed in a hot and copper sky after the albatross is killed.
quotations.analysis: The stanza repeats its first line as its third, so that the surrounding sea is enacted by the surrounding words. The two lines between are the boards shrinking and the absence of drink, both facts about dryness; the ocean is described entirely by what it will not do.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part II

quotations.text: Day after day, day after day, We stuck, nor breath nor motion, As idle as a painted Ship Upon a painted Ocean.
quotations.context: The calm, before the water-snakes and the death-fires.
quotations.analysis: The doubled phrase is stasis performed in metre. The simile makes the ship a picture, and a picture is something looked at rather than lived in, which is exactly the crew’s condition: they are becoming spectators of their own deaths.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part II

quotations.text: Instead of the Cross the Albatross About my neck was hung.
quotations.context: The crew hang the dead bird on the Mariner.
quotations.analysis: The rhyme of Cross and Albatross makes the substitution audible: a sailor would wear a crucifix, and this crew has replaced one sign of sacrifice with another. The passive verb keeps the Mariner as the thing acted upon, which is how he describes himself for the rest of the tale.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part II

quotations.text: Alone, alone, all all alone, Alone on the wide wide Sea; And Christ would take no pity on My soul in agony.
quotations.context: The crew are dead; the Mariner is left on the deck among their bodies.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of alone in one line and the doubled wide in the next: the stanza has almost no vocabulary, which is what isolation sounds like. The refusal of pity from Christ is stated flatly, without complaint, and prepares the surprise of the blessing that comes from nowhere a few stanzas later.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part IV

quotations.text: O happy living things! no tongue Their beauty might declare: A spring of love gusht from my heart, And I blessed them unaware!
quotations.context: Watching the water-snakes in the shadow of the ship.
quotations.analysis: The turning point of the poem is an act the Mariner did not decide to perform; the word unaware is repeated in the next line to make sure the reader notices. He could not pray before because he had willed the killing; he can pray after because the love was not willed at all.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part IV

quotations.text: He prayeth best who loveth best All things both great and small: For the dear God, who loveth us, He made and loveth all.
quotations.context: The Mariner’s parting words to the wedding-guest.
quotations.analysis: The moral is small, plain and hymn-like, and readers since Coleridge himself have wondered whether it is adequate to the poem it closes. Its very inadequacy is instructive: the tale has shown a universe of Death, Life-in-Death and dice, and the teller can only offer the guest a rule he could have learned in church.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part VII

quotations.text: He went, like one that hath been stunned And is of sense forlorn: A sadder and a wiser man He rose the morrow morn.
quotations.context: The last stanza. The guest turns from the bridegroom’s door.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends on its listener, not its teller, and on a comparative rather than a conclusion: sadder, wiser, than what he was. The feast he was going to is still audible. The stanza also tells the reader what a poem is supposed to do to them, which is the closest Coleridge comes to a preface of his own.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Ancient Mariner’, Part VII

quotations.text: Five years have passed; five summers, with the length Of five long winters! and again I hear These waters, rolling from their mountain-springs With a sweet inland murmur.
quotations.context: The opening lines.
quotations.analysis: The number is said three times in a line and a half, and each time it is measured by a different unit, years, summers, winters. Time is being weighed before the landscape is described, and the exclamation mark on long winters admits that the interval has been felt as loss before the poem tries to make it a gain.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey’

quotations.text: While with an eye made quiet by the power Of harmony, and the deep power of joy, We see into the life of things.
quotations.context: The end of the passage on the blessed mood in which the body is laid asleep.
quotations.analysis: The eye is made quiet by something outside it; the grammar keeps the self passive right up to the verb. The sentence has been suspending the breath and the blood for six lines, and lands on the smallest words in the poem, life and things, as though the revelation could only be stated plainly or not at all.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey’

quotations.text: For I have learned To look on nature, not as in the hour Of thoughtless youth, but hearing oftentimes The still, sad music of humanity, Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power To chasten and subdue.
quotations.context: After the account of the boyish self who bounded over the mountains like a roe.
quotations.analysis: Music is the surprising noun: humanity is heard rather than seen, and heard as something quiet. The two negatives, nor harsh nor grating, define the sound by what it is not, and chasten and subdue are verbs of discipline, so the recompense for lost rapture is described as a kind of correction.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey’

quotations.text: A presence that disturbs me with the joy Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused, Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, And the round ocean and the living air, And the blue sky, and in the mind of man A motion and a spirit, that impels All thinking things, all objects of all thought, And rolls through all things.
quotations.context: The centre of the poem: what the speaker has felt in the place of his lost boyish appetite.
quotations.analysis: The presence is never named as God, and disturbs is the verb chosen for it. The list of dwellings moves from setting suns to the mind of man in one sentence, so that the mind is placed among the elements rather than above them; the final clause has no object at all, only motion.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey’

quotations.text: Knowing that Nature never did betray The heart that loved her;
quotations.context: The prayer for the sister, in the poem’s final movement.
quotations.analysis: This is the collection’s creed stated as a past-tense fact, never did, and it is spoken to another person rather than to the reader. The rest of the sentence lists what the creed has to withstand, evil tongues, rash judgments, the sneers of selfish men, which is a surprisingly social list for a poem about a river.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written a Few Miles Above Tintern Abbey’

quotations.text: “How many are you then,” said I, “If they two are in Heaven?” The little Maiden did reply, “O Master! we are seven.”
quotations.context: The adult tries a last time, after the child has described the two deaths.
quotations.analysis: The adult’s question contains its own answer, if they two are in Heaven, and the child ignores the condition and repeats the number. Master is the only deference in the exchange, and it is deference to a man who has just lost an argument with an eight-year-old.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘We Are Seven’

quotations.text: ’Twas throwing words away: for still The little Maid would have her will, And said, “Nay, we are seven!”
quotations.context: The last stanza, after the adult has insisted that the dead are dead.
quotations.analysis: The narrator concedes defeat in the first line and the poem gives the child the last word anyway, in an extra line: this stanza has five lines where every other has four. The form itself makes room for the answer the adult cannot accept.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘We Are Seven’

quotations.text: Come forth into the light of things, Let Nature be your teacher.
quotations.context: The evening reply to the friend who wanted William back among his books.
quotations.analysis: Light of things is a strange phrase: light is usually what falls on things, not what they are made of. Teacher answers the book-learning of the first poem, so the pair together argue that education is a matter of where you stand rather than what you read.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Tables Turned’

quotations.text: Sweet is the lore which Nature brings; Our meddling intellect Misshapes the beauteous forms of things; —We murder to dissect.
quotations.context: The penultimate stanza.
quotations.analysis: The stanza moves from sweet lore to murder in four lines, and the last half-line is set off with a dash as though the speaker had surprised himself. Dissect was a word from the anatomy schools; applied to intellect it turns analysis into a post-mortem, which is an argument the Preface takes up in prose.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Tables Turned’

quotations.text: To her fair works did Nature link The human soul that through me ran; And much it griev’d my heart to think What man has made of man.
quotations.context: The second stanza, in a grove where pleasant thoughts bring sad ones.
quotations.analysis: The line that closes the stanza returns to close the poem, and it never says what man has made. The noun is used twice with no adjective between, so that the indictment is entirely in the verb made: humanity as a manufacture, set against the flowers that enjoy the air they breathe.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Lines Written in Early Spring’

quotations.text: O Reader! had you in your mind Such stores as silent thought can bring, O gentle Reader! you would find A tale in every thing.
quotations.context: The narrator breaks off to tell the reader that no tale will be related.
quotations.analysis: The apostrophe to the reader arrives exactly where a ballad would supply its incident, and replaces the incident with an instruction. Every thing is printed as two words, which restores the stress to thing: the claim is that any object, a root or a stump, is enough if the mind brings its stores.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Simon Lee, the Old Huntsman’

quotations.text: I’ve heard of hearts unkind, kind deeds With coldness still returning. Alas! the gratitude of men Has oftener left me mourning.
quotations.context: The last stanza, after the old man’s tears at a single blow of the mattock.
quotations.analysis: The expected moral is that ingratitude wounds; the poem says the opposite, that gratitude does. Unkind and kind sit side by side to be crossed out, and mourning is left as the rhyme for returning, so the ending sounds like a couplet but works like a reversal.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Simon Lee, the Old Huntsman’

quotations.text: “The Cocks did crow to-whoo, to-whoo, And the Sun did shine so cold.” —Thus answered Johnny in his glory, And that was all his travel’s story.
quotations.context: Johnny’s answer to his mother’s demand that he tell them true.
quotations.analysis: His report is accurate: the owls did call all night and the moon did shine. The poem calls it glory without irony, and gives it the only quoted speech of Johnny’s in nearly five hundred lines, which makes the idiot the one narrator in the volume who says exactly what he saw.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Idiot Boy’

quotations.text: And this I know, full many a time, When she was on the mountain high, By day, and in the silent night, When all the stars shone clear and bright, That I have heard her cry, “Oh misery! oh misery! Oh woe is me! oh misery!”
quotations.context: The last stanza. The narrator sets what he knows against what he has heard.
quotations.analysis: After twenty-two stanzas of rumour the narrator finally states something he has witnessed, and it is a sound rather than a fact. The cry is all he has, and he gives it as the poem’s last line; the case against Martha Ray rests on a noise heard on a mountain.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Thorn’, stanza XXIII

quotations.text: She lived unknown, and few could know When Lucy ceased to be; But she is in her Grave, and oh! The difference to me.
quotations.reference: She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways
quotations.context: The last stanza of a twelve-line poem.
quotations.analysis: Ceased to be is the flattest possible phrase for dying, and the poem ends on a noun, difference, with no adjective to say what kind. The grief is measured by a gap between two states rather than described, and the exclamation oh! is the only place the speaker’s voice breaks.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways’

quotations.text: A slumber did my spirit seal; I had no human fears: She seemed a thing that could not feel The touch of earthly years. No motion has she now, no force; She neither hears nor sees, Rolled round in earth’s diurnal course With rocks and stones and trees!
quotations.reference: She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways (the untitled poem printed after it)
quotations.context: The whole of the eight-line poem printed without a heading after ‘She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways’.
quotations.analysis: The first stanza is past tense and the second present, and the death happens in the white space between them. She is never named. Rolled round with rocks and stones and trees can be read as consolation, she is part of the earth now, or as horror, she is a thing that cannot feel; the poem gives no punctuation to decide.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), printed without heading after ‘She Dwelt Among th’ Untrodden Ways’

quotations.text: Then, dearest Maiden! move along these shades In gentleness of heart; with gentle hand Touch⁠—for there is a Spirit in the woods.
quotations.context: The last lines, after the boy has dragged down the hazel boughs and felt the intruding sky.
quotations.analysis: The poem turns without warning from a memory to an instruction, and to a listener who has not been mentioned before. Touch is isolated by a dash, so the verb is given as an act of care to set against the earlier crash and merciless ravage; the Spirit is asserted, not shown.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Nutting’

quotations.text: There is a comfort in the strength of love; ’Twill make a thing endurable, which else Would break the heart:⁠—Old Michael found it so.
quotations.context: After the news that Luke has gone to the bad and fled beyond the seas.
quotations.analysis: The general statement comes first and the particular man is attached to it after a dash, as proof. Endurable is not consolation; the sentence says the heart would otherwise break, and the next lines show what enduring looks like, a man walking to a sheep-fold for seven years.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Michael’

quotations.text: ’Tis not forgotten yet The pity which was then in every heart For the Old Man⁠—and ’tis believed by all That many and many a day he thither went, And never lifted up a single stone.
quotations.context: The neighbours’ memory of Michael in the years after Luke’s ruin.
quotations.analysis: The line everyone remembers is a negative: the poem’s climax is something not done. It is reported through the pity of the neighbourhood, believed by all, so the image reaches the reader the way it reached Wordsworth, as local testimony about a heap of stones by a brook.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘Michael’

quotations.text: As in the eye of Nature he has lived, So in the eye of Nature let him die.
quotations.context: The last two lines of the poem, after the argument against the workhouse.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends in a plea rather than a description, let him, and the balanced clauses make the death a right earned by the life. Eye is the word Tintern Abbey used for perception; here it is Nature that does the seeing, and the beggar asks only to remain visible to it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), ‘The Old Cumberland Beggar’

quotations.text: For all good poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: but though this be true, Poems to which any value can be attached, were never produced on any variety of subjects but by a man, who being possessed of more than usual organic sensibility, had also thought long and deeply.
quotations.context: From the 1800 Preface, on the purpose of the poems.
quotations.analysis: The famous half of the sentence is the first clause; the qualification after the colon is the part Wordsworth cared about, and it says the opposite of spontaneity. Overflow is a liquid image, but the sentence ends with a man who has thought long and deeply, and the collection is the product of both.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), Preface to the 1800 edition

quotations.text: I have said that Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity
quotations.context: From the 1800 Preface, near its end, on how a poem is made.
quotations.analysis: Recollected is the key term, and Tintern Abbey is its demonstration: five years between the feeling and the poem. The sentence goes on to say that the tranquillity gradually disappears as the emotion is contemplated, so the theory is not about calm but about a second feeling produced by remembering the first.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text (1800 two-volume text), Preface to the 1800 edition

timeline.label: William Wordsworth born at Cockermouth
timeline.detail: In the north-western corner of the Lake District he would return to in 1799.

timeline.label: Samuel Taylor Coleridge born at Ottery St Mary
timeline.detail: The youngest of a Devon vicar’s large family, later of Christ’s Hospital and Cambridge.

timeline.label: Wordsworth and Coleridge meet in Bristol
timeline.detail: Both were in the city’s radical and Unitarian circles in the year of the Treason Trials’ aftermath.

timeline.label: The Wordsworths move to Alfoxden, near Coleridge at Nether Stowey
timeline.detail: A year of daily walks in the Quantocks in which most of the 1798 poems were written.

timeline.label: The Ancient Mariner begun on a November walk
timeline.detail: Planned as a joint poem to pay for a walking tour; Wordsworth contributed the albatross and the dead men working the ship and then withdrew.

timeline.label: Tintern Abbey composed on a walking tour of the Wye in July
timeline.detail: The title dates it to the thirteenth of the month; Wordsworth said no line was altered after the walk.

timeline.label: Lyrical Ballads published anonymously in Bristol by Joseph Cottle
timeline.detail: Late in the year, with the Mariner first and Tintern Abbey last, and a short Advertisement in place of a preface.

timeline.label: Wordsworth and Dorothy winter in Goslar
timeline.detail: The coldest winter of the century, by Wordsworth’s account, and the season of the Lucy poems and the first draft of The Prelude.

timeline.label: The two-volume second edition, dated 1800
timeline.detail: With the Preface, a wholly new second volume ending in Michael, and the Mariner moved to the back of the first.

timeline.label: Third edition, with the Preface enlarged
timeline.detail: The passage asking what is meant by the word Poet was added here.

timeline.label: Biographia Literaria and Sibylline Leaves
timeline.detail: Coleridge gives his own account of the collaboration and its division of labour, and reprints the Mariner with a marginal prose gloss.

timeline.label: Coleridge dies at Highgate
timeline.detail: After eighteen years in the household of the surgeon James Gillman.

timeline.label: Wordsworth becomes Poet Laureate
timeline.detail: Succeeding Southey, the third of the Lake poets.

timeline.label: Wordsworth dies at Rydal Mount; The Prelude published
timeline.detail: The autobiographical poem begun at Goslar appears in the year of his death.

places.name: Tintern Abbey, Wye valley
places.note: The ruin the poem is written a few miles above, revisited in July 1798 after five years.

places.name: Alfoxden, Holford
places.note: The house under the Quantocks where the Wordsworths lived in 1797–98 and most of the first volume was written.

places.name: Nether Stowey
places.note: Coleridge’s cottage, three miles from Alfoxden; the Mariner was planned on walks from here.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: Where the poets met in 1795 and where Joseph Cottle printed the 1798 volume.

places.name: Esthwaite Water
places.note: The lake of Expostulation and Reply, near Wordsworth’s school at Hawkshead.

places.name: Grasmere
places.note: The vale of Michael; Green-head Gill runs down to the village from the north-east.

places.name: Goslar
places.note: The Harz town where Wordsworth and Dorothy spent the winter of 1798–99 and the Lucy poems were written.

criticalViews.position: The Preface as the key to the poems
criticalViews.summary: The oldest way of reading the book is through Wordsworth’s 1800 argument: poems of common life in the real language of men, feeling giving importance to action rather than the reverse. On this view the collection is a demonstration of a theory of diction, and its plainness is its point.
criticalViews.counter: The 1798 volume had no such theory, only a short Advertisement, and Coleridge later argued in Biographia Literaria that the Preface described a practice Wordsworth’s best poems did not follow.

criticalViews.summary: Coleridge’s account of the division of labour, the supernatural made credible against the ordinary made new, has encouraged readers to treat the Mariner as a separate enterprise sharing a binding with Wordsworth’s experiments. Wordsworth’s own 1800 note listing the poem’s defects lends support.
criticalViews.counter: The Mariner and Tintern Abbey were placed side by side in 1800, and both are poems about a mind changed by something it did not choose; the seam is less clean than the story of the collaboration suggests.

criticalViews.summary: Readings since the 1980s attend to what the poems are about rather than how they sound: beggars, vagrants, discharged soldiers, shepherds losing land, the workhouse, the war with France. The Old Cumberland Beggar takes a position in a live debate about poor relief, and Michael is a story about a mortgage.
criticalViews.counter: The poems keep returning to the observer’s feelings rather than the sufferer’s remedy, and the Preface is explicit that the feeling is the subject; a reader who wants policy will find the book evasive.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the Mariner belong in Lyrical Ballads?
plan: Set out the oddity: a supernatural ballad in archaic diction opening a book that advertises itself as experiments in ordinary language.
Use Coleridge’s later account of the division of labour and Wordsworth’s move of the poem to the back of the 1800 volume as evidence that both poets felt the seam.
Then look for what the poem shares with the rest: a listener who cannot choose but hear, a speaker compelled to tell, a change that happens unaware.
Compare the blessing of the water-snakes with the moments of unearned feeling in Simon Lee and Nutting.
Conclude on the 1800 placing, beside Tintern Abbey: two accounts of a mind altered by an experience it can only report.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The poems are about the people who watch, not the people who suffer.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Observers, the poor and the reader’s position
plan: Take Simon Lee as the test case: the narrator promises no tale, gives one blow of a mattock, and ends with his own mourning.
Contrast The Old Cumberland Beggar, which argues on the beggar’s behalf but describes him entirely from outside.
Use We Are Seven and Anecdote for Fathers to show adults learning from children and being the subject of the poem while doing so.
Set Michael against the pattern: a whole household followed to its end, with the narrator standing back.
Weigh whether the observer’s discomfort is evasion or the collection’s honest subject, using the Preface’s claim that feeling gives importance to action.

essayQuestions.question: What does Tintern Abbey claim memory can do?
plan: Begin with the counting of five years and the exclamation on long winters: the poem starts by admitting an interval felt as loss.
Trace the first claim, that remembered forms have given sensations sweet in lonely rooms, and the larger claim of the blessed mood in which we see into the life of things.
Read the account of the boyish self, all in all, appetite, dizzy raptures, and the abundant recompense offered for it.
Turn to the sister: the speaker finds his past in her voice and asks her to remember the place for him, which makes memory a thing entrusted to another person.
Connect the poem to the Preface’s emotion recollected in tranquillity and decide whether the poem believes its own consolation.

essayQuestions.question: How does the collection use narrators who do not know what happened?
essayQuestions.focus: Testimony, rumour and the reader as judge
plan: Open with The Thorn: a narrator who has measured the pond and the moss-heap and reports everything else as what some say.
Compare We Are Seven, where the narrator has the facts and loses the argument, and The Idiot Boy, where the only truthful report is Johnny’s.
Show how the Mariner is a tale within a tale, teachable but not verifiable, with a listener as its only proof.
Use Michael, where the story is attached to a heap of stones and vouched for by the neighbourhood, as the collection’s model of good testimony.
Conclude on what the reader is asked to do: weigh the witness as well as the evidence, which is the Preface’s programme carried out in form.

discussionQuestions: The Mariner shoots the albatross and the poem gives no reason. Would a reason make the poem better or worse?
The child in We Are Seven wins the argument. Does the poem agree with her?
Simon Lee promises a tale and refuses to tell one. What does the reader get instead, and is it enough?
Wordsworth moved the Mariner from the front of the book to the back in 1800. What changes when a collection opens with Expostulation and Reply instead?
Michael goes to the sheep-fold for seven years and never lifts a stone. Is that failure, grief or fidelity?

related.why: The poem on its own, with the marginal gloss Coleridge added in 1817, for comparison with the bare 1798 text printed here.
The conversation poems and Kubla Khan, written in the same Quantock years, and the rest of the partnership’s other half.
Mary Shelley’s Walton quotes the Mariner on his voyage north; the novel is the first great reading of the poem.
The blank verse Wordsworth inherits for Tintern Abbey and Michael, and the poem he measured his own long work against.
